name: Biacromial / clavicle width

card.summary: The bone-based width of the shoulder girdle, which looksmaxxers treat as a fixed frame limit that muscle can only add to.
card.aka: bone-set shoulder width, clavicle length, biacromial breadth
card.note: Mostly a measurement concept; no studies found on appearance effects.

quick.overview:
Biacromial width is the distance between the outer points of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length is the length of the collarbones. Looksmaxxers treat both as the skeletal limit on how wide the shoulders can look.

Community threads ask what counts as a good clavicle or bideltoid width and compare measurements, often in inches and at a stated height.
quick.mechanism: The clavicle is a horizontal strut between the sternum and shoulder blade. Males usually have longer clavicles than females, and the bone finishes ossifying around age 21 to 25. Muscle such as the deltoids sits on top of this frame and adds soft-tissue width.
quick.risks: Measuring is harmless, though community comparison can feed body-image concern. Surgery to alter the clavicle is a separate topic with its own risks, covered in the clavicle lengthening osteotomy article.

lead: Biacromial width, the span across the outer points (acromion processes) of the two shoulder blades, and clavicle length are discussed in looksmaxxing as the bone-set limits on shoulder width. Members commonly say that training can add muscle on the outside of this frame but cannot change the skeleton.[1][11]

The appearance point is the shoulder-to-waist and shoulder-to-hip proportion. A wider bone frame gives the shoulders a broader base, and people then build deltoids, lats and upper back on top of it to make the frame look broader and more tapered. Knowing which part of the width is skeletal and which is trainable is how members decide where to put effort.[1][3]

Wikipedia describes the clavicle as an S-shaped long bone lying horizontally between shoulder blade and sternum, about 15 cm long, and reports that males usually have longer and larger clavicles than females and that the bone starts ossifying in the fifth and sixth weeks of gestation but finishes only around age 21 to 25.[2] Research on the look of the shoulders comes mainly from studies of the shoulder-to-hip ratio, in which broader male shoulders relative to the hips have been rated more attractive in several samples.[12][13] No clinical studies of biacromial or clavicle width as a looksmaxxing target were found.

chain: Clavicle and acromion set the bone width of the shoulder girdle
Deltoid, lat and upper-back muscle adds width on top of the frame
Broader-looking shoulders relative to waist and hips
angle.text: People measure clavicle and biacromial width to understand their frame, then train deltoids and back muscles to add visible width on top of it. The bone itself is described as fixed after skeletal maturity.

infobox: Males usually have longer, larger clavicles[2]
Not the bone; muscle adds soft-tissue width

paras: The clavicle acts as a rigid strut that holds the shoulder and arm away from the trunk, allowing a wide range of arm movement. It has a medial sternal end, a lateral acromial end and a shaft; its lateral end forms by intramembranous ossification and its medial end by endochondral ossification.[2] The acromion is a process of the scapula that continues from the scapular spine and meets the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint; Wikipedia describes it as the summit of the shoulder.[11]

Biacromial width is the distance between the two acromion processes, so it reflects both the length of the clavicles and the width and angle of the shoulder blades and the chest they sit on. Clavicle length is a related but separate figure. Forum members also use bideltoid width, the span across the outer surface of the two deltoids, which includes muscle and is therefore trainable.[1]

The deltoid has three heads, with the anterior head arising from the lateral third of the clavicle, the middle head from the acromion and the posterior head from the scapular spine; all converge on the humerus and the muscle forms the rounded contour of the shoulder.[3] Soft tissue therefore contributes to total shoulder width beyond the bone.

In a study of 748 males and 252 females cited on Wikipedia, clavicle length grew by roughly 6 mm in males and 5 mm in females between the 18 to 20 and 21 to 25 age groups.[2] Wikipedia also reports that the clavicle is the first bone to start ossifying and one of the last to finish, that its shape varies more than most long bones, and that the left clavicle is usually longer and weaker than the right.[2] The acromion develops from four ossification centres, most of which fuse between about 15 and 18 years.[11]

A looksmax.org thread asks what a good clavicle width and bideltoid size are. The poster, 5 feet 6 inches tall, reports an 18 inch clavicle width and 20 inch bideltoid width and says the frame still looks narrow to them, and replies trade figures and targets.[1] The thread notes that average bideltoid width is not well documented and that clavicle width data are hard to find. Members use these metrics to decide how much of their shoulder appearance can be changed by training and how much is skeletal.

A second looksmax.org thread has a teenager listing a biacromial breadth of 52.5 cm alongside height and neck, hip and waist measurements and asking whether breadth can still increase and by what methods.[5] Another thread has users comparing tape-measured figures of about 21 cm and noting that typical values of about 18 to 19 cm are quoted from memory.[6] On T Nation, a lifter reported that he and his partner gained 1.5 to 2 inches of biacromial width after adding certain back exercises to their routines.[7] Posters often differ on measurement method, such as whether a tape or caliper was used or whether muscle was included, which affects comparability.

The ideas feed into the wider gymmaxxing discussion, where shoulder and upper-back training is the main way to change the visible width, and into the separate entry on clavicle lengthening osteotomy, a surgical option that some members raise when they consider the bone itself the limit.

A 2020 speed-dating study by Sidari, Lee, Murphy, Sherlock, Dixson and Zietsch in Social Psychological and Personality Science measured the bodies of 539 students and had them rate partners across 2,161 face-to-face interactions of three minutes each. Men with broader shoulders were rated as having more attractive bodies, while the authors noted that the associations were weak and reflected first impressions only.[12]

A 2023 EEG study by Pazhoohi, Arantes, Kingstone and Pinal in Archives of Sexual Behavior showed 48 participants avatars with small, medium and large shoulder-to-hip ratios; both male and female participants rated larger ratios as more attractive, and male avatars produced more distinct neural responses than female ones.[13] A 2017 study of photographs found that rated upper-body strength explained most of the variance in men's rated bodily attractiveness, with height and leanness adding to it.[14] None of these studies measured bone width separately from muscle, so they do not distinguish skeletal from trainable contributions.

Anthropometric research measures shoulder breadth in various populations. A 2022 systematic review of 26 studies covering 317,202 children and adolescents found that biacromial diameter, alone or combined with other bone breadths, was used in 27 percent of reports of body frame size, with the frame index the most common measure; the authors reported no unified measurement or reference cut-offs.[8] A 1989 study of 162 men used biacromial breadth among the predictors in equations for lung function.[9]

Clinical literature on the clavicle focuses largely on fractures and their surgical management; Wikipedia calls the clavicle the most commonly broken bone.[2][4] On training, a 2010 randomized study of grip width and forearm orientation on lat pull-down muscle activity addresses how back exercises load the lats, which add width on top of the skeleton, rather than skeletal width itself.[10]

Wikipedia's hypertrophy article reports that muscle growth depends mainly on mechanical tension, total volume and progressive overload, and that hypertrophy is faster during puberty and generally stops at full growth in the late teens, which is why members stress that muscle, not bone, is the changeable part of shoulder width.[15]

No studies found on biacromial or clavicle width as an appearance target. Related research covers anthropometric frame-size measures, clavicle fractures, and shoulder-to-hip ratio and attractiveness ratings.[4][8][12][13]

lore.intro: Clavicle and bideltoid numbers are posted on looksmax.org for comparison, with some users setting large target figures for the frame.[1]

claims.claim: Clavicle width sets the ceiling for how wide the shoulders can look.
claims.believers: Users say the bone is the part they cannot train and that it drives the 'twink' versus broad impression.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the clavicle's length differs by sex and finishes growing in the early twenties.[2] No study tested its role in perceived attractiveness separately from muscle.

claims.claim: Specific bideltoid numbers (for example 24 inches) define a high-status frame.
claims.believers: Some posters name large figures as targets.[1]
claims.experts: No population norms or attractiveness thresholds for such figures were found in published sources.

claims.claim: Broad shoulders relative to the waist and hips make a man look more attractive.
claims.believers: Members treat shoulder width as a core part of the V-taper and a reason to measure the frame.[1][5]
claims.experts: Speed-dating and EEG studies report that larger shoulder widths or shoulder-to-hip ratios are rated as more attractive, with weak associations in the speed-dating data.[12][13]

claims.believers: A T Nation poster said he and his girlfriend gained 1.5 to 2 inches of biacromial width after adding specific back work, and some users believe lats and rear-delt work can widen the frame.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports the clavicle finishes ossification around 21 to 25 years and grew about 5 to 6 mm between age groups in one study; no cited study tested whether training changes biacromial breadth.[2]

claims.claim: Adolescents and young adults can still widen the shoulder frame.
claims.believers: Teenagers on looksmax.org ask whether biacromial breadth and height can still increase at 18 or 19.[5]
claims.experts: The clavicle is one of the last bones to finish ossifying, at about 21 to 25 years, so some growth is documented up to then.[2]

claims.claim: Measurements posted online are comparable with each other.
claims.believers: Threads compare figures such as 52.5 cm or 21 cm and quote typical values of 18 to 19 cm from memory.[5][6]
claims.experts: The anthropometry review reports no unified measurement protocol or reference cut-offs for biacromial diameter in the literature it examined.[8]
